title: Edith Stein
hookLine: a Jewish-born philosopher who became a Carmelite nun and was killed at Auschwitz

lines: A BOOK OFF A FRIEND'S SHELF.
cards: A guest in a friend's house can't sleep, so she pulls a book off the shelf: the life of Teresa of Ávila, the Spanish nun, in her own words.
The guest is a philosopher, sharp, trained to take ideas apart, and for years she has had no religious faith at all. She reads through the night.

When she closes the book, tradition says, she tells herself: this is the truth. Her name is Edith Stein. She was born into a Jewish family, and the road that night opens will end in a place no one would choose.

teach.b: Edith Stein grew up in an observant Jewish home with a mother she loved deeply.
As a young woman she left faith behind for philosophy, studying under Edmund Husserl, a founder of phenomenology, the careful study of experience as it's lived.
She wrote on empathy: how we can know what another person goes through.

After that night with Teresa, she was baptized a Catholic, which grieved her mother. Years later she entered a Carmelite convent, the order Teresa had reformed, and took a new name, Sister Teresa Benedicta of the Cross.
She never stopped seeing herself as a daughter of the Jewish people. As Nazi persecution grew, her order moved her to a convent in the Netherlands for safety.

Then the Dutch Catholic bishops publicly protested the deportation of Jews, and the occupiers struck back by arresting Catholics of Jewish birth. Edith was taken with her sister Rosa, who had also become Catholic.

teach.h: COME, WE ARE GOING FOR OUR PEOPLE.
teach.b: By the account of witnesses, Edith took Rosa's hand and said, come, we are going for our people. She was murdered at Auschwitz.

In a letter she had compared herself to Queen Esther, who stood before the king to plead for her people. In the King James Bible, Esther says: "let my life be given me at my petition, and my people at my request."
The Catholic Church has named her a saint and a martyr. Some Jewish voices have asked, fairly, that this not blur a plain fact: the Nazis killed her because she was born a Jew.
Both are part of her story, and honoring her means holding all of it.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Teresa Benedicta of the Cross each August, and Carmelites honor her as one of their own; her philosophical writings are studied in universities, and some Catholic and Jewish groups remember her together in Holocaust remembrance.

games.q: you're Edith, being taken from the convent with your sister Rosa. Rosa is frightened. what do you say?
o: take her hand: come, we are going for our people.
tell her it's a mistake and you'll be home soon.
games.why: by witnesses' account, Edith took Rosa's hand and said, come, we are going for our people.

practice: Think of someone you tend to describe with one label: the convert, the one who left, the difficult one.
Let the rest of their story come in, where they started, what they lost, what they kept, who they still belong to, until the label gets smaller and the person bigger.
If you pray, pray for that whole person; if you don't, just hold them, whole.
